item.title: Dual-Spectrum Thermal Cameras: Principles, NVR Integration, and the Market
item.description:
Two in the morning, a fence line on a business campus. A visible-light camera with IR illuminators shows you the ten meters its light reaches — beyond that, black. A chemical tank farm is worse: the camera is supposed to watch, around the clock, not “is anyone there” but “which tank is running hot” — point a visible camera at a steel tank and it tells you nothing.

Thermal imaging fixes exactly these two scenes: it needs no light at all, receiving infrared radiation emitted by the objects themselves, so image brightness maps directly to temperature. But thermal has its own blind spot — no texture, no readable faces, no license plates. So the industry bolts two lenses into one housing: thermal finds things, visible light identifies them. That’s a dual-spectrum (bi-spectrum) camera.

item.title: Code-Generated Promo Videos (6): TTS Selection Guide — 31 Engines and Services Compared
item.description:
Part 2 of this series used edge-tts to generate voiceovers, and Part 5 laid out the TTS technology evolution. This is the final installment — a complete selection guide for when your project outgrows edge-tts. What are the 31 TTS engines and services on the market, and how do you choose among them?

We organize the selection landscape into three layers: free open-source engines (run locally, zero licensing cost but with GPU deployment overhead), free cloud tiers (ready out of the box with usage limits), and paid services (ready out of the box + SLA + advanced capabilities). These are not strictly hierarchical — an open-source engine on self-hosted GPU can be cheaper long-term than paid cloud, while cloud services offer convenience that self-deployment can’t match. The choice ultimately depends on your budget, team capacity, and timeline.
